ARE.story:
In September 2019 the Group of Eminent Experts on Yemen, a panel set up by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate abuses by the forces fighting in Yemen, reported that personnel from the United Arab Emirates at Al-Bureiqa had raped a boy. The same report found that other forces in Yemen had raped boys and girls, and the panel said its figures were only a small sample.

Telegram, a messaging app, has its operational centre in Dubai and its legal home in Tortola, in the British Virgin Islands. On 24 August 2024 its founder, Pavel Durov, was arrested at Le Bourget airport in France. Four days later a Paris investigating judge, a judge who directs a criminal investigation in France, placed him under formal investigation on charges that included suspected complicity in running a platform that allowed images of child sexual abuse, and refusing to give information to the authorities. A BBC investigation that month found that Telegram had not joined NCMEC, the US centre that receives reports of abuse images, or the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), a British charity that finds and removes them, and had ignored repeated requests to join. The IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse images on Telegram since 2022. In December 2024 it announced that Telegram would use its list of digital fingerprints of known abuse images to find such material in the public parts of the app.

The UAE also took part in police work against online abuse. In 2015 it was one of ten members of the Virtual Global Taskforce, a group of police agencies, that arrested 303 people suspected of sharing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims.

The UAE hosts the operating centre of a platform whose founder was placed under formal investigation in France in 2024, and there are no representative surveys from its region to show how many children there are abused online.

BEL.story:
In 1992 Marc Dutroux was released early from a 13.5-year sentence for rape, over the objections of a prosecutor and a psychiatrist. In 1995 and 1996, while on parole, he kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19. His mother wrote to the authorities in 1995 that he was holding two girls, and police treated him as a prime suspect from June 1995, yet they took 14 months to arrest him. They missed chances, including voices heard in his cellar and videotapes nobody reviewed, and rivalry between the Gendarmerie and the judicial police slowed the search.

Dutroux was arrested in August 1996. In October 1996 hundreds of thousands of Belgians joined the White March in Brussels to protest against police and judicial failures. A parliamentary inquiry chaired by Marc Verwilghen criticised the police investigation, and Belgium later reorganised its police forces. In 2004 Dutroux was sentenced to life. Witnesses told investigators of abuse parties involving Dutroux and prominent people, but prosecutors dismissed the statements, and the claims of an elite network remain unproven.

The Catholic Church in Belgium ran its own commission, chaired by Godelieve Halsberghe, from 2000. It upheld 32 of 33 formal complaints, but 31 were past the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a case. In April 2010 Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges resigned after admitting he had abused his nephew, and a new church-backed commission led by Peter Adriaenssens received 475 complaints in six months. In June 2010 police raided church premises and seized the commission's files, and its members resigned; an appeals court later ruled the raids disproportionate. A committee of the Chamber, the lower house of parliament, then reported in 2011 that abuse had occurred in every sector of the church and recommended a compensation body, which was set up in 2012. After a 2023 television series, 'Godvergeten', a Chamber commission of inquiry reported in May 2024 with 137 recommendations.

By 2024 parliament was still asking for the church's records to be opened to police and courts, and for a study of lifting the time limit on old cases.

CAN.story:
In December 1975 the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary opened an investigation into abuse at the Mount Cashel orphanage in St John's, and the police chief closed it nine days later. In 1976 the Justice Department ordered the police report rewritten, and in 1977 the Deputy Minister of Justice said further action was not warranted. Nothing more was done until 1989, when the Hughes Inquiry, a royal commission with the power to require evidence, was set up to examine how Newfoundland's criminal justice system had responded. It found that officials had transferred offenders and covered up abuse. Eleven Christian Brothers, members of a Catholic religious order, were convicted, and in 1996 Newfoundland paid C$11.5 million in compensation.

The federal government funded residential schools, run by churches, to assimilate First Nations, Métis and Inuit children, and about 150,000 children attended them. Under a settlement reached in 2007, tens of thousands of claims of sexual and serious physical abuse at the schools were compensated.

Two priests of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, a Catholic missionary order, who had worked in Nunavut, were accused of abusing Inuit children and moved to Europe. Eric Dejaeger had already served five years in the early 1990s for abusing children in Baker Lake. In 1995, when he was about to be charged over abuse in Igloolik, he fled to Belgium, and Oblate officials later acknowledged they knew he was leaving. He lived in Oblate houses there for 16 years despite an international warrant. After he was returned in 2011 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 sex crimes against Inuit children. Johannes Rivoire, a French Oblate, left for France in January 1993. Canada issued a warrant for him in 1998 over abuse of Inuit children, and in 2022 issued another and asked France to extradite him, which the French authorities refused. A 2024 review commissioned by the Oblates concluded that he had assaulted six children. He died in France that year without trial.

Where an accused priest left Canada, whether he was ever tried depended on whether the country he went to would send him back.

COD.story:
In 2010 the UN human rights office published its Mapping Exercise report on the most serious violations committed in DR Congo between 1993 and 2003. It described the apparent systematic use of rape and sexual assault, allegedly by all the armed forces, against women and girls. All sides used child soldiers, who were murdered, raped and tortured in military camps, and the national army was among the 12 parties the UN Secretary-General had named for recruiting children.

In 2012 the International Criminal Court (ICC), which tries individuals for war crimes, convicted Thomas Lubanga of the armed group UPC of conscripting children under 15 and using them as fighters in Ituri in 2002 and 2003, and sentenced him to 14 years; sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at his trial but was not charged. In 2019 the court convicted Bosco Ntaganda of 18 counts from the same years in Ituri, including rape, sexual slavery and the use of children under 15.

In 2004 UN investigators in Bunia found that sexual contact with peacekeepers of MONUC, the UN mission in DR Congo, happened 'with regularity', usually in exchange for food or small sums of money, and that many cases involved girls under 18, some as young as 13. A UN report in 2005 found that about 45% of the 105 allegations recorded across all UN missions in 2004 involved sex with people under 18. From 2018 to 2020, during the response to Ebola in North Kivu and Ituri, a commission appointed by the World Health Organization (WHO) identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of them WHO employees, many of whom offered jobs in exchange for sex. The youngest person it heard was a 13-year-old girl who said a WHO driver raped her.

In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls in DR Congo, by armed groups including M23 (68) and CODECO (63) and by the national army (47), and the abduction of 815 children. Peacekeepers accused of abuse there can be tried only by their own countries, and the UN reported in 2025 that few such cases had been finalised.

ECU.story:
In 2017 the families of pupils abused at the Academia Aeronáutica Mayor Pedro Traversari, a school in Quito known as AAMPETRA, campaigned for action. Forty-one children had been abused there. In response, Ecuador's National Assembly, the national parliament, set up an occasional commission, a temporary committee with members from several parties, to review cases of sexual violence in schools from 2013 to 2017. Its report, approved unanimously on 16 February 2018, found negligence by public institutions, the Ministry of Education and judicial authorities, and concluded that former ministers had not acted. Human Rights Watch, an international human rights organisation, later analysed government data and counted 4,221 pupils who suffered sexual violence in schools between 2014 and May 2020.

Abuse by Catholic clergy has been counted by journalists. A months-long investigation by Visión 360, a programme on the Ecuadorian channel Ecuavisa, counted 103 complaints of sexual abuse involving Ecuadorian clergy, with cases in Guayas, Pichincha, Azuay and Los Ríos, including complaints concerning Fr César Cordero and Fr Luis Intriago. Victims' families said the church hierarchy refused to share information or to file complaints with prosecutors itself, which went against the National Assembly commission's report. A survivors' association demanded that these crimes be made imprescriptible, meaning they could be prosecuted at any time, as voters had approved in a referendum.

The National Assembly found in 2018 that the state had failed to act on sexual violence in schools, and government data later showed thousands of pupils affected up to 2020. For abuse by clergy, the count so far comes from journalists, and families say the church has not reported cases to prosecutors.

GBR.story:
Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958. Two police investigations in his lifetime produced no charges, Surrey Police dropped an inquiry in 2007–09, and in December 2011 the BBC shelved a report about him by its own Newsnight programme. In October 2012 London's Metropolitan Police opened Operation Yewtree, and in 2013 it recorded 214 crimes by him. Later inquiries found 72 victims linked to the BBC and victims aged 5 to 75 in hospitals of the state health service.

In Rotherham, children's-home managers and youth workers reported the sexual exploitation of children from the early-to-mid 1990s, and the researcher Angie Heal warned officials from 2002 to 2007. A rape reported in 2001 ended with the suspect released without charge, and action against the abusers began only in 2010. An independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited in the town between 1997 and 2013, and called the failures of the council and the police 'blatant'. The National Crime Agency, the national agency for serious crime, then took over the case; it has identified about 1,150 potential victims, and 39 people have been convicted. In Oxfordshire a review in 2015 found that police did not believe the girls and treated them as if they had chosen their situation.

Medomsley Detention Centre in County Durham held young male offenders from 1961 to 1988. Neville Husband, the officer who ran its kitchens, was convicted of sexual offences in 2003 and 2005, and eight former staff were jailed. In November 2025 the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman, the independent investigator of complaints about prisons, found that what the Prison Service, the police and the Home Office knew of the abuse had been 'ignored and dismissed'.

From June 2026 people in England and Wales who were abused as children can sue however long ago the abuse happened, unless the defendant shows a fair trial is impossible. The National Crime Agency is now investigating allegations that former South Yorkshire Police officers abused children, and no finding has yet been made.

IDN.story:
In its final report, Chega!, published in 2005, Timor-Leste's Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation found that at least 4,000 children had been forcibly taken from their families and moved illegally to Indonesia during the Indonesian occupation, which ended in 1999. Indonesian military units took children, some of whom they used as child soldiers or servants, and Islamic organisations took children and converted them. The children were often renamed and lost contact with their families. The commission and a joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste Commission of Truth and Friendship recommended a commission to search for the missing children, but it was never created.

Children from Indonesia were also sent abroad for adoption. In 2021 a Dutch commission of inquiry found serious violations in adoptions to the Netherlands from countries including Indonesia between 1967 and 1997/98, and the Dutch government suspended all intercountry adoption on 8 February 2021.

In July 2025 West Java police said a syndicate of recruiters, caretakers and document forgers had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, for 11–16 million rupiah each, some 'reserved while still in the womb'. The syndicate prepared fraudulent family cards, the household registration document, and passports in Pontianak. Thirteen people were arrested, six babies were rescued, and police asked Interpol for help to trace the adopters.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says sexual exploitation of children by visiting foreigners is prevalent in the Riau Islands, which border Singapore, and that women and girls are coerced into commercial sex notably in Batam. It says tourists from the Middle East pay more than $700 for week-long 'contract marriages' in Puncak, Bogor, with girls as young as nine, a practice the government tacitly accepted, and that corruption and complicity significantly impeded efforts against trafficking.

In 2025 babies were still being sold abroad with forged papers, and foreign visitors were still paying for girls in the Riau Islands and Puncak. The children taken from Timor-Leste have never been searched for by the commission that was recommended.

ISL.story:
In early November 2012 an investigative commission of the Catholic Church in Iceland, chaired by Hjördís Hákonardóttir, reported on Landakotsskóli, the church's school, and on the church's summer camps. It confirmed that the school's principal, Rev. Ágúst Georg, and a teacher, Margrét Müller, had abused pupils. Of 30 former pupils and summer-camp children it questioned, 8 said they had been sexually abused and 27 described mental abuse. It also found that Bishop Joannes Gijsen had destroyed a letter from a man who said the priest had abused him.

In December 2015 the Althing, Iceland's parliament, passed Act No. 117/2015, which extended the state's compensation scheme for people abused in institutions to cover Landakotsskóli.

Iceland also hosts abuse material online. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes images of child sexual abuse, took action against 7,455 web addresses hosted in Iceland, 2 percent of all those it acted on that year. Iceland was also among the countries involved in Operation Stream, the 2025 action led by Bavarian police with Europol, the EU's police agency, against Kidflix, a paid site for streaming abuse videos with 1.8 million users.

The account of abuse at Landakotsskóli comes from a commission the church set up itself, and the state's response was to extend compensation to former pupils. Abuse material hosted in Iceland was still being found and removed in 2025.

KOR.story:
From 1953 to 2008 South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad for adoption, through four agencies authorised by the government. In 1974 the government tried to stop adoptions to Scandinavia, but Swedish, Danish and Norwegian diplomats sent nine pleas and the adoptions resumed. In 2025 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state inquiry body, found violations in at least 56 of the cases brought by 367 adoptees. The agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand and registered children with known parents as orphans, and the state had treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to welfare at home. President Lee Jae-myung apologised in October 2025.

In 2005 a teacher at Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students alerted human rights groups and was fired. An investigation that year found that six people at the school had sexually harassed or raped at least nine students. Two escaped punishment because the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for prosecution, had expired. After a 2011 film about the case, 'Silenced', the National Assembly passed the 'Dogani Law', removing that deadline for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled people.

In 2019 students and journalists exposed the Nth Room and Doctor's Room, chatrooms on the messaging app Telegram where operators blackmailed women and girls into making sexual images and sold access to them. At least 74 victims, 16 of them minors, were exploited there. In 2020 a court sentenced Cho Ju-bin, who ran the Doctor's Room, to 40 years, and the law was changed to punish possessing and viewing such material. In August 2024 a journalist revealed Telegram chatrooms where users shared sexual deepfakes, faked images, of female students and teachers. By late September, police had handled more than 800 deepfake sex crime cases in 2024, against 156 in 2021, and most victims and perpetrators were teenagers.

The state has accepted responsibility for the adoptions, and the laws on abuse in schools and online were changed after the Dogani and Nth Room cases became public. Abuse through Telegram chatrooms continued after the 2020 convictions.

MLT.story:
In 1991 the Catholic bishops of Malta set up a Response Team, chaired by Judge Victor Caruana Colombo, to deal with complaints of abuse by clergy. In April 2010 the Maltese Curia, the church's central administration, said the team had handled 45 cases of abuse of minors by priests over 19 years. Nineteen were dismissed as unfounded, 13 were still open, four priests had been found guilty and removed from ministry, and two priests had died. By the same month the church in Malta had recorded 84 allegations.

Some cases reached the criminal courts. Fr Charles Pulis was sentenced to six years and Fr Godwin Scerri to five years for abusing boys at St Joseph Home, a church children's home run by the Missionary Society of St Paul. Donald Bellizzi received three years in 2020.

Children from Malta were also sent abroad. Under child migration schemes, British and Maltese children were sent to institutions in Australia, among them homes run by the Christian Brothers, a Catholic religious order, at Bindoon, Castledare, Clontarf and Tardun in Western Australia. In August 2001 a committee of the Australian Senate reported that of 207 former child migrants who wrote to it, 38 described sexual abuse, 24 of them in Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia. The committee described 'systemic criminal sexual assault' and predatory behaviour by a large number of Christian Brothers over a long period.

The figures on abuse by clergy in Malta come from the church's own Response Team and a few criminal convictions. The abuse of Maltese child migrants was examined in Australia, together with that of British children.

NRU.story:
The Regional Processing Centre on Nauru was a detention centre for people seeking protection as refugees. Australia funded and ran it, using contracted guards and staff. Families with children were held there.

On 11 February 2015 the Australian Human Rights Commission, the national body that monitors human rights, tabled its inquiry 'The Forgotten Children' in the federal parliament. It counted 33 reported sexual assaults in Australian immigration detention, including the Nauru centre, between January 2013 and March 2014, and said the vast majority involved children.

In March 2015 a review by Philip Moss, commissioned by the Australian government, reported that it was aware of three rape allegations at the centre, one involving a minor. It confirmed that a guard had demanded to see a female detainee naked in exchange for extra shower time with her young child, and concluded that guards were possibly trading marijuana with detainees for sexual favours. In April 2015 staff at the centre wrote an open letter alleging multiple instances of sexual abuse of women and children, and said the Australian government had known of the alleged abuses for more than 18 months. A Senate select committee, a group of senators appointed to examine one subject, reported on 31 August 2015 under the title 'Taking responsibility: conditions and circumstances at Australia's Regional Processing Centre in Nauru'.

The official record of what happened to children held on Nauru comes from Australian reviews and inquiries in 2015, which recorded allegations from staff and detainees and confirmed some of them.

SAU.story:
In its 2026 update, Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys of the public into global estimates of child abuse, had representative surveys from only 60 countries. Too few came from the Middle East and North Africa, the region that includes Saudi Arabia, to represent it, so the centre's estimates of how many children are sexually exploited through phones and the internet do not rest on surveys from the region.

Most of what is recorded about children exploited in Saudi Arabia comes from reports about other countries. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking in Ethiopia says traffickers exploit Ethiopian women and children in Saudi Arabia in forced begging, sometimes through organised begging rings. The same department's 2025 report on Indonesia says tourists from the Middle East pay for short 'contract marriages' with girls as young as nine in Puncak, West Java.

Children brought to Saudi Arabia from abroad appear in other governments' reports, and there are no representative surveys from the region to measure the abuse of children who live there.

SYR.story:
On 3 August 2014 Islamic State, an armed group based in Syria, attacked Sinjar in northern Iraq and captured Yazidi women and children. It moved them to holding sites in Tal Afar and Mosul and then took women and girls to Raqqa in Syria, where they were sold. In June 2016 the UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found that Islamic State had committed genocide. Women and girls, some as young as nine, had been sold at market and held in sexual slavery, and boys had been forced into its training camps. At that date more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria.

On 15 March 2018 the same commission published 'I lost my dignity', covering March 2011 to December 2017. It found that most parties to the conflict had committed sexual violence. Women and girls were raped in detention, at checkpoints and in house raids, and male detainees, boys among them, were sexually tortured. The commission named government forces and the militias allied with them as the worst offenders. It also found that Islamic State forced girls and women to marry its fighters. In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 14 children in Syria by the Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement, government forces and the YPG/YPJ, often to recruit and use them.

In March 2016 Lebanese security forces freed as many as 75 Syrian women from two brothels, Chez Maurice and Silver-B, in Jounieh. Chez Maurice had been raided in late 2011, when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found trapped there, and had reopened after about three months. The US State Department's 2025 report says Syrian girls in Türkiye are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies and then held in domestic servitude and sex trafficking, and that in Jordan Syrian refugee women and girls have been sold into forced marriages.

The UN was still verifying abductions of children inside Syria in 2024, and Syrian refugee girls were still being forced into marriage abroad in 2025. Thousands of the Yazidi women and children taken in 2014 remain missing.

USA.story:
In 1974 the bishop of the Diocese of Lafayette, in Louisiana, made Fr Gilbert Gauthe a Boy Scout chaplain despite allegations that he had abused altar boys. In 1976 Gauthe was sent for therapy and then returned to work. He later admitted abusing 37 children, and in 1985 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years. His was the first widely publicised prosecution of a priest for abuse in the United States.

At Pennsylvania State University, a 1998 report to the university police about the assistant football coach Jerry Sandusky was not prosecuted. In 2001 a graduate assistant's report of seeing Sandusky with a boy in a shower went to the coach Joe Paterno and university officials, who did not tell the police. Sandusky was convicted in 2012 of abusing 10 boys, and in 2017 the athletic director, a vice-president and the university's president were convicted of child endangerment. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997. The FBI was told in July 2015 but did not act, and the Justice Department's internal watchdog found that at least 70 more athletes were abused between the reports to the FBI and his arrest. By his final hearing, 265 victims had been identified.

In 2005 Palm Beach police in Florida investigated the financier Jeffrey Epstein and identified about 35 girls, but a state grand jury, a panel of citizens that decides on charges, returned only a single count of soliciting prostitution. In 2007 the federal prosecutor's office under Alexander Acosta agreed not to bring federal charges against Epstein and several suspected co-conspirators and kept the agreement from the victims. Epstein served 13 months of an 18-month state sentence.

When states proposed lengthening the legal deadlines for suing over childhood abuse, Catholic organisations, insurers and the Scouts lobbied against the changes. At least 41 Catholic dioceses and orders, the Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics filed for bankruptcy facing abuse claims.

No national inquiry into abuse in American institutions has been held; the investigations have been by state attorneys general and grand juries, or commissioned by the church.
